text.p: Wienerberger Baustoffindustrie, the world's biggest brickmaker, said on Thursday it would turn in a substantially higher pretax profit this year after weathering a gruelling 1996 with minor bruises.

Reporting preliminary results for 1996, Wienerberger said pretax profit fell 13 percent to 1.3 billion schillings ($113 million) due to prevailing limp demand in Europe's construction sector, which in turn was exacerbated by an unusually harsh and long winter.
"Due to marked price declines in Austria and Germany our traditionally most profitable division, bricks, experienced substantially reduced profitability," Wienerberger said in a statement.
In the brick division, pretax profit tumbled to 650 million schillings from 882 million.
But Wienerberger said it was confident the worst was behind and forecast a 25 percent jump in group pretax profit for the current year.

"Our optimism for 1997 derives from our strong market presence, our cost leadership and the yet untapped market potential in Eastern Europe -- all of which should result in an above average profit increase," the brickmaker said.

The company was "satisfied" with its pretax profit which it said came in line with its forecast of between 1.2 to 1.4 billion, although chief executive Erhard Schaschl had recently been gunning for 1.4 billion.

The result and forecast were also within market expectations, which saw Wienerberger's margins eroded by the severe winter and sluggish construction, but with profits later buoyed by the benefits of an aggressive acquisition spree.

Wienerberger said its 1996 acquisition of Belgium's biggest brickmaker was a decisive factor in strengthening its performance, with Terca Bricks contributing 325 million schillings to group pretax profit and 2.4 billion to sales.

Overall, Wienerberger's earnings before interest and tax slipped to 1.66 billion schillings from 1.674 billion in 1995. Operating profit was largely unchanged at 1.7 billion, while sales climbed to 14.6 billion from 12.9 billion.
Analysts agreed that Wienerberger was well placed to benefit from an eventual upturn in European construction.

Investmentbank Austria recommends the brickmaker as a long-term buy, forecasting earnings per share rising to 118 schillings this year and to 140 schillings in 1998. Last year, EPS tumbled to 103 schillings from 168 in 1995.
Wienerberger shares finished Thursday's session unchanged at 2,190 schillings. The results were reported after the market closed. ($1=11.53 Schilling)
